checkpoint_name: English Guided Option Selection Rewrite Design
question: Do these rewritten guided option examples sound like usable live-call wording, including sparse discourse markers, or do they still need rewriting?
source_rules: Do not repeat what the customer already said unless explicitly needed.
Answer the actual fit or difference question.
Use approved plan feature facts, not invented differences.
Steer toward the better option when known customer facts support it.
Keep wording shorter and more human.
Preserve autonomy without repeatedly saying neither or not now.
Use light persuasion when the customer is uncertain but still engaged.
Separate option selection from payment handling.
payment_rule: For now, option selection must not collect payment on the call. The agent may explain the approved campaign payment path if the campaign profile defines it.
naturalness_rule: Do not add random fillers. Treat discourse markers as a future spoken-naturalness rule that must be sparse, context-aware, and blocked in sensitive boundary statements.

examples.title: Direct choice
examples.customer_turn: So do I choose the $29 option or the $59 option?
examples.proposed_response: I mean, if you only need [feature X] and [feature Y], start with $29. If [feature A] matters too, $59 fits better.
examples.review_focus: Answer fit directly without repeating that one option is cheaper.

examples.title: Fit is unclear
examples.customer_turn: I can see both paths, I am just not sure which one fits me.
examples.proposed_response: Based on what you said, $59 sounds stronger if [feature A] saves you time. If not, $29 is the safer start and you can upgrade later.
examples.review_focus: Steer from customer facts while preserving the upgrade path.

examples.title: Recommendation request
examples.customer_turn: Which route would you suggest for someone like me?
examples.proposed_response: Honestly, like, if your main issue is [customer pain], I would lean $59 because it adds [feature A] and [feature B]. If budget matters more, start $29.
examples.review_focus: Allow a recommendation without pretending to choose for the customer.

examples.title: Explain the difference
examples.customer_turn: What is the real difference between the $29 option and the $59 option?
examples.proposed_response: $29 covers [feature X], [feature Y], and [feature Z]. $59 adds [feature A] and [feature B], so it fits better if you need [customer goal].
examples.review_focus: Answer the real difference using approved plan facts.

examples.title: Decide later
examples.customer_turn: Can I choose later instead of deciding on this call?
examples.proposed_response: Yes. I can send the differences in writing and keep both options open for the follow-up.
examples.review_focus: Keep deferral short and avoid saying the same thing twice.

examples.title: Neither feels right
examples.customer_turn: I'm not sure either is right.
examples.proposed_response: I get that, you know, it may just mean we should match the plan to [customer goal] first, then see whether $29 or $59 makes sense.
examples.review_focus: Use acknowledgement plus light persuasion instead of ending the opportunity.

examples.title: Payment path
examples.customer_turn: If I pick one, can I pay now?
examples.proposed_response: No payment on this call. I'll send the companyname.com email with the link, and you can review the plan and finish registration there.
examples.review_focus: Explain the approved campaign payment path without collecting payment.

examples.title: Start cheaper, upgrade later
examples.customer_turn: Could I start smaller and change later if it works?
examples.proposed_response: You can start with $29 if [feature X] covers enough. If you later need [feature A] or [feature B], we can move you to $59.
examples.review_focus: Use the upgrade path as a selling bridge when campaign rules allow it.
